hints: Start by thinking about where the GFP gene comes from in the jellyfish cell and what form that information is in - DNA or mRNA - and what you need to copy it.
Next think about the carrier DNA that will take the gene into the pig - what must be cut open first, and with what type of enzyme to give matching sticky ends.
Finally think about which enzyme seals the new gene into the opened carrier by rebuilding the backbone between nucleotides.
walkthrough:
Get a DNA copy of the GFP gene**
You are sitting with the jellyfish cell. It makes GFP mRNA when the gene is expressed. Reverse transcriptase uses that mRNA as a template to make cDNA, so you now have a stable double-stranded DNA version of the GFP gene without introns, ready for transfer.

Open the vector with the same cutter**
The carrier is usually a plasmid vector. Restriction endonuclease cuts it open at specific recognition sequences to create sticky ends. The same enzyme is used to cut out the GFP cDNA so the ends are complementary and can base-pair together.

Seal the gene in**
DNA ligase then joins the GFP gene into the vector. It catalyses formation of phosphodiester bonds between the sugar-phosphate backbones, producing recombinant DNA that can be introduced into pig cells to make a transgenic pig.

Final answer: Restriction endonuclease cuts vector/plasmid; reverse transcriptase makes cDNA from GFP mRNA; DNA ligase joins gene to vector by forming phosphodiester bonds in the sugar-phosphate backbone.

hints: Think about what is special about green fluorescent protein under a microscope filter compared to most other pig genes.
Think about what you would see if Cas9 worked and deleted that gene, compared to if it failed.
walkthrough:
A gene you can see**
Most gene deletions give no visible change. GFP is different because when expressed it fluoresces green under a filter. It works as a marker, so presence of the functional gene is directly observable in the blastocyst.

Deletion means loss of signal**
If Cas9 nuclease successfully causes a deletion in the GFP target, expression is prevented and no fluorescence is seen. So counting fluorescent versus non-fluorescent blastocysts gives a quick, clear measure of efficiency.
Final answer: GFP acts as a marker gene; loss of fluorescence shows the GFP gene has been deleted, success is easily seen.

hints: In the control row, compare the number seen under the filter with the total number seen under white light and think about what fraction x 100 gives.
walkthrough:
Use the control row**
Under white light all blastocysts are counted: 68. Under the filter only those expressing GFP show up: 46. Percentage transgenic $= (46 / 68) \times 100 = 67.6\%$, about $68\%$.
Final answer: $(46 / 68) \times 100 = 67.6\%$ (accept 68%).

hints: Think about the cross: non-transgenic ova crossed with sperm from a male with one copy per somatic cell, so what proportion of zygotes should receive the gene.
walkthrough:
Expect 1 in 2**
The mother has no copies, the father has one copy per cell so is heterozygous for the transgene. On average half the sperm carry it, so you expect $50\%$ transgenic zygotes. Your calculated $67.6\%$ is higher than this $50\%$ expectation.
Final answer: Higher than expected, as 50% of offspring expected to inherit GFP gene from heterozygous male.

hints: Think about which statistical test compares observed categorical counts with expected counts to test for significant difference.
walkthrough:
Observed versus expected**
You have observed numbers of transgenic and non-transgenic and an expected 1:1 ratio. The $\chi^2$ test is the standard test for significance of difference between observed and expected categorical data.
Final answer: Chi-squared ($\chi^2$) test.

hints: Look down Table 5.1 at the white-light column as concentration rises - what does fewer blastocysts tell you about toxicity.
Now look at the filter column for all three injected groups - what does zero tell you about deletion efficiency at even the lowest dose.
Combine those two trends to pick the dose that keeps deletion complete while keeping survival highest.
walkthrough:
Balance killing and deleting**
You need a concentration that deletes GFP in all cases but kills as few zygotes as possible. White-light counts fall from 40 at 10, to 24 at 20, to 15 at 50 $\text{ng mm}^{-3}$, so toxicity increases with concentration.

Check efficiency**
Under the filter all injected groups show 0 fluorescent blastocysts, compared to 46 in the control. Even $10 \text{ ng mm}^{-3}$ gives complete loss of fluorescence, so it is just as effective as 20 and 50.

Choose the lowest effective dose**
Best is $10 \text{ ng mm}^{-3}$ because it gives the highest survival (more blastocysts, less toxic) while still showing no blastocysts under the filter, meaning all survivors have deleted GFP.

Final answer: $10 \text{ ng mm}^{-3}$; gives more blastocysts surviving (least toxic) and still 0 blastocysts seen under filter, so as successful as higher concentrations with all blastocysts having deleted GFP.

hints: Compare the band positions in lanes 1-4 with lanes 5-6 and the marker on the right - what size is each band.
Use the stated normal gene size of 6 kbp to work out how much DNA is missing in the four piglets.
Link loss of that DNA to the cell surface protein and what the virus needs to get into cells.
walkthrough:
Read the gel**
Lanes 5 (surrogate mother) and 6 (normal pig) both show a band at 6 kbp, the normal target gene size. Lanes 1-4 (four pigs born after Cas9) all show a lower band at 4 kbp only. That means the technique worked in 4 out of 4, so 100% successful.

Measure the deletion**
$6 \text{ kbp} - 4 \text{ kbp} = 2 \text{ kbp}$ deleted or lost from the gene. The gene is now shorter and cannot code for the normal cell surface protein.

Explain resistance**
That cell surface protein is essential for PRRSV to infect pig cells. Without the normal protein the virus cannot enter cells, so pigs 1-4 should show resistance to PRRSV.

Final answer: Lanes 1-4 show 4 kbp fragment while lanes 5-6 show 6 kbp; technique 100% successful in all four pigs; 2 kbp deleted so no normal cell surface protein made, so PRRSV cannot infect cells/pigs, giving resistance.
